Notes: Year Established basis: Leibner (Settlement and History in Hellenistic, Roman, and Byzantine Galilee, 2009, pp. 214-216, 221, 278-279): the Franciscan excavations and his survey show Migdal was 'first established only during the Hasmonean period around the late second/early first century BCE'; 'in all the excavations conducted at the site, the earliest finds belong to the Hasmonean period'; 'it is obvious that the settlement was Jewish from the outset, as already in 53 BCE it was involved in Jewish rebellion'. Leibner links its foundation to Hasmonean settlement of Jews in eastern Galilee. Year = c. 100 BCE (midpoint of late 2nd/early 1st c. BCE). Founding of a Jewish town; no count. David Gurevich (Bible and Interpretation, Aug. 2018, 'Magdala's Stone of Contention'): 'Archaeologically, Magdala was first settled during the Hasmonean rule'; he describes the settlers as coming from Judea. Date = Hasmonean foundation c. late 2nd/early 1st c. BCE (c. 100 BCE). Foundation of a Jewish town; no count.

Hasmonean coins: Gvaryahu's BMCR review (2025.03.15) of B. Callegher, Coins and Economy in Magdala/Taricheae from the Hasmoneans to the Umayyad Period (2023): 'Most of the coins are Hasmonean (140-37 BCE) and Roman'; random site finds 'dropped on the ground during daily life', with a statistical analysis of coins of Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE). Year = Hasmonean-period midpoint (-90). Indicates an active settlement under Hasmonean rule; no count.

IAA excavation 2009-2013 (Avshalom-Gorni and Najar, Hadashot Arkheologiyot 125, 2013): meagre Hellenistic remains (Stratum 4); numismatists 'identified Hasmonean coins and coins from the first century CE'; settlement 'established in the Hellenistic period'. Year = Hasmonean-period midpoint (-90). Presence of the early (Hasmonean) settlement; no count.

Event: the Roman commander (Cassius, named in the preceding section) 'fell upon Taricheae' and took it, and 'carried about thirty thousand Jews captives', killing Pitholaus, follower of Aristobulus (Josephus, Antiquities 14.120 [14.7.3]). Date c. 53/52 BCE (Leibner dates the pro-Aristobulus revolt to 53 BCE). The 30,000 are captives, apparently including rebels gathered from the region, not a count of residents - Population blank. Shows a substantial Jewish town already in the mid-1st c. BCE.

De Luca and Leibner, 'A monastery in Magdala (Taricheae)?', Journal of Roman Archaeology 32 (2019), first page: 'Several sources point to the town's importance and its large Jewish population in the Early Roman period'; cites capture and 'enslavement of 30,000 people (Jos., AntJ 14.120)' after the Roman conquest, and its role as capital of a toparchy in the 1st c. CE (BJ 2.252; AntJ 20.158-59). Year = Early Roman period midpoint (63 BCE-70 CE = 4). Qualitative 'large Jewish population'; no count. (PDF text extracted locally.)

Literary attestation of an individual: 'Mary, called Magdalene' (Luke 8:2), a Jewish woman named after Magdala, among Jesus' followers c. 30 CE (c. date of Jesus' Galilean ministry). Leibner (2009: 227) notes Ruf's view that the epithet implies she no longer lived at Migdal. Individual originating from the town; no count.

Modern archaeological estimate DERIVED from Leibner (2009): site area of Tarichea/Migdal in the Early Roman period = 90 dunams (site entry p. 214; p. 221: 'Tarichea, which during this period was 90 dunams'); Leibner's density coefficients for eastern Galilee = 16-35 persons per dunam (higher end for semi-urban sites 'e.g., Migdal'), central value 26 (pp. 307-308). 90 x 16 = 1,440; 90 x 35 = 3,150; 90 x 26 = 2,340 (Leibner's own averaging method). Leibner does not print this town figure himself; it is his area x his coefficients. Leibner calls the town Jewish from its Hasmonean foundation, so total = Jewish population. Leibner on Josephus' 40,000 (War 2.608): 'even if the numbers are exaggerated, one still gets the image of a town with a considerable population'. Year = 1st c. CE (50). [Review fix: Population 2340 moved to Notes; derived by the agent (90 dunams x 26 persons/dunam); Leibner gives the area and coefficients but no figure for Magdala]

Bible History Daily (N. Steinmeyer, 15 Dec 2021): 'Magdala was a large Jewish settlement during the first century'; 'Its population is estimated to have been around 30,000.' Unattributed popular figure, apparently derived from Josephus, and far above what the 90-dunam site area (Leibner) allows - left out of Population as uncertain. Year = 1st c. CE (50).

Bible History Daily (M. Dospel, 2022): 'The population of Taricheae grew to approximately 30,000 by the mid-first century', as Josephus 'implies in his account of the Roman suppression of the revolt' (i.e. derived from Josephus' captive/casualty figures, which included many refugees) - Population blank. Also mentions four miqva'ot and the 2009 synagogue. Year = mid-1st c. CE (50).

Synagogue 1 (IAA excavation, Avshalom-Gorni and Najar, HA-ESI 125, 2013): 'a Jewish settlement dating to the beginning of the Roman period'; the synagogue 'is the earliest one discovered so far in the Galilee'; its carved stone with a seven-branched menorah 'is the earliest menorah from the Second Temple period to be discovered outside of Jerusalem'. Stratum 3 pottery dates 'from the year 50 CE until the end of the first century CE'. Organized Jewish community with a synagogue. Year = 1st c. CE (50).

Synagogue 2 (University of Haifa excavation 2021, A. Erlich and D. Avshalom-Gorni), reported by Sci.News: a second Second Temple-period synagogue; 'Finding two synagogues less than 200 m apart in a locality of several thousand residents...' (excavators' characterization; 'several thousand' is not a precise figure, so Population blank). Two synagogues indicate a sizeable organized Jewish community. Year = 1st c. CE (50).

Miqva'ot (Magdala Archaeological Project, Universidad Anahuac, 2010-11; A. Garza-Diaz, World History Encyclopedia, 2018): 'the first ritual baths (miqva'ot) next to the Sea of Galilee fed by underground water'; Magdala was 'a wealthy Jewish town in the Lower Galilee'; synagogue 'dates from the 1st century'. Jewish ritual-purity installations in domestic contexts. Year = 1st c. CE (50).

Event: Nero, in the first year of his reign (54 CE), gave Agrippa II 'a certain part of Galilee, Tiberias, and Tarichae' (Josephus, Antiquities 20.158-159; War 2.252 adds 'with the toparchies to them belonging'). Tarichea as capital of a toparchy under Agrippa II; no count.

Josephus, Life 188: 'I also fortified, in the Lower Galilee, the cities Taricheae, Tiberias, Sepphoris...' - Josephus, as rebel commander in Galilee (66-67 CE), fortified Tarichea as a 'city' (polis) and used it as his base. Year = 66 CE (start of the revolt). No count.

Josephus, War 2.608 (riot over the Dabaritta spoils, 66 CE): Josephus relied on 'the people of Taricheae, and about forty thousand in number'. Ancient figure: a crowd of supporters at the hippodrome, and Leibner (2009: 221) treats Josephus' 40,000 as possibly exaggerated - Population blank. See also Life 132-154 (same episode; 'the people of Taricheae and the strangers').

Encyclopaedia Judaica (via Jewish Virtual Library): 'among its prominent citizens were Jannaeus son of Levi and Dassion' (Josephus, Life 131; War 2.597), during the revolt (66 CE); Magdala 'was walled on the land side and contained a stadium'. Named Jewish residents; no count.

Event: Roman capture of Taricheae by Titus (autumn 67 CE; Josephus, War 3.462-505 [3.10.1-5]). Josephus distinguishes 'the natural inhabitants', who 'were not disposed to fight' and had not consented to the war, from 'the foreigners, which were very numerous'; 'There was also a great slaughter made in the city' until Titus slew 'the authors of this revolt'. No count of residents.

Event: after the naval battle on the lake opposite Taricheae (67 CE), 'The number of the slain, including those that were killed in the city before, was six thousand and five hundred' (Josephus, War 3.531 [3.10.9]). Death toll including many refugees/foreign fighters - Population blank.

Event: Vespasian's tribunal at Taricheae (67 CE; Josephus, War 3.532-542 [3.10.10]) 'to distinguish the foreigners from the old inhabitants'; the old and useless 'a thousand and two hundred' were killed; 'six thousand of the strongest' young men sent to Nero; the rest sold 'for slaves, being thirty thousand and four hundred', besides those given to Agrippa. Captive and casualty counts (largely outsiders who had gathered at Tarichea, per Josephus) - Population blank.

Leibner (2009: 220, 223-224): Suetonius (Titus 4.3) calls Tarichea and Gamla 'urbes Iudaeae validissimae' ('strong Jewish towns'); Vespasian spared the permanent inhabitants and killed or sold the outsiders, the Romans 'apparently did not destroy the town itself'; Franciscan excavations found 'no destruction level or gap in settlement during the second half of the first century CE' (Loffreda 1976). Agrippa later sold the spared inhabitants into slavery (Leibner's reading of War 3.540-542). Jewish town survives the conquest in part; no count. Year = 67 CE.

IAA excavation (HA-ESI 125, 2013): 'the quarter and the synagogue were probably deserted at the time of the Great Revolt'; the Roman conquest 'resulted in the abandonment and destruction of the site' (the excavated quarter; a coin of 80 CE lay on the synagogue's collapsed ceiling). Abandonment of part of the Jewish town in 67 CE; not stated that no Jews remained - Population blank.

Garza-Diaz (World History Encyclopedia, 2018): after the Roman victory 'A massacre of the town's residents then followed', but 'Magdala was not completely destroyed as Josephus wrote' and 'the archaeological findings do not give information regarding how complete the destruction was'. Year = 67 CE. Partial destruction; no count.

Coins of the First Jewish Revolt: Wikipedia (Magdala) reports that at the excavated buildings 'Many of the coins dated to the time of the first Jewish revolt against Rome (66 - 70 CE)'; a collapse layer 'supports Josephus's narrative of the Roman destruction'. Year = c. 68 (midpoint of 66-70). Presence of Jewish residents during the revolt; no count. (Wikipedia used as last resort.)

Agoranomos lead weight found at Migdal (Leibner 2009: 226-227, citing Qedar 1986-87 and Kushnir-Stein 2002): dated to year 23 of 'the great king Agrippa' (Kushnir-Stein's reading; = 71/72 CE on Agrippa II's era of 49 CE; other readings give year 43, c. 61/2 or later) naming the market officials 'Iaesaias (son of) Mathias and Aianimos (son of?) Monimos' - Iaesaias son of Mathias (Isaiah son of Mattathias) is a Jewish name. Leibner attributes the weight to Tarichea's own market. Suggests Jewish municipal officials after the conquest; date c. 72 CE, uncertain. No count.
